summary.text: Embryonic development is the stage in which an animal embryo forms, starting when a sperm cell fertilizes an egg cell.
The fertilized egg, a single cell called a zygote, divides without significant growth in a process called cleavage, forming a morula, then a blastula, then a gastrula.
The gastrula goes on to form organs, and the embryo then moves to a next stage that varies by species, such as a fetus or a larva.

facts.value: Cell divisions with no significant growth

items.prompt: In one embryo every cell of the early cluster divides; in another, the division skips the yolky region so only some cells divide. Which pairing names these?
items.explain: Holoblastic cleavage divides all the cells derived from the zygote, while meroblastic cleavage divides some but not all, because the furrow does not enter the yolky region.

items.prompt: Right after one sperm fertilizes an egg, the egg's membrane potential rapidly depolarizes and then returns to normal. What does this achieve?

options.label: It begins the first cell division straight away
It helps stop extra sperm from fertilizing the egg
It makes the zygote grow to twice its size
It signals the cells to begin forming organs

items.explain: This quick change is the fast block, one of two ways of preventing polyspermy.

items.prompt: Which stage develops directly from a dense ball of at least sixteen cells?
items.explain: The ball of cells is the morula, and it develops into a blastula; the gastrula comes after the blastula.

items.prompt: An embryo's cells divide again and again, yet the whole cluster stays the size of the original zygote. Why?

options.label: Cells die as fast as they divide
Division pauses until the organs form
Only the outer cells are able to divide
The divisions happen with no significant growth

items.explain: This kind of division is called cleavage: the zygote splits into more and smaller cells without significant growth.

items.prompt: In an amniote's morula, the cells sort into an outer layer and an inner cluster. Which part goes on to form the embryo itself?
items.explain: The trophoblast does not contribute to the embryo proper; the inner cell mass is where the embryo develops.

items.prompt: In one species the egg is fertilized outside the female's body; in another, inside it. Which pairing names these?
items.explain: Depending on the species, fertilization happens within the female (internal) or outside her body (external).

beats.title: One cell becomes an animal
beats.hook: A fertilized egg splits again and again without growing, yet ends up as a whole animal.

beats.prompt: Put these early stages of an animal's development in order.
beats.explain: Fertilization comes first, then cleavage produces the morula, which develops into a blastula, which then develops into a gastrula.

beats.prompt: A zygote divides again and again by mitosis. How big is the resulting cluster of cells compared with the original zygote?
beats.explain: Cleavage is cell division with no significant growth, so the cluster is the same size as the original zygote.

choices.label: About the same size as the zygote
Twice as large after every division
choices.feedback: It tempts because the cell count doubles, but the cells only get smaller; the cluster does not grow.

choices.label: Much larger, since each new cell grows to full size
choices.feedback: It tempts because more cells seems to mean more mass, but these divisions happen with no significant growth.

beats.prompt: Match each cleavage pattern to what it does.

right.label: Divides some but not all cells
Divides all cells from the zygote

beats.explain: Holoblastic cleavage divides every cell, meroblastic only some because the furrow does not reach the yolky region, and basal phyla show the radial holoblastic form.

beats.prompt: Sort each event into the block against extra sperm that it belongs to.

left.label: Happens immediately after a single sperm fertilizes the egg
Membrane potential depolarizes, then returns to normal
Release of calcium causes the cortical reaction
Enzymes are released from cortical granules

beats.explain: The fast block is a quick change in membrane potential, while the slow block is the calcium-triggered cortical reaction that hardens the outer membrane.

beats.idea: A zygote follows a sequence of stages, each built on the last, from cleavage to a gastrula that goes on to form organs.

paragraphs.heading: From egg to embryo
paragraphs.text: Animal embryonic development, also called embryogenesis, is the stage when an animal is an embryo. It starts when a sperm cell fertilizes an egg cell, or ovum. The fertilized egg becomes a single cell called a zygote. In mammals the term mostly covers the early stages before birth, while the words fetus and fetal development name the later ones.

paragraphs.heading: Fertilization
paragraphs.text: Fertilization is the joining of gametes to make a new organism; in animals, a sperm fuses with an ovum. Depending on the species, this happens inside the female's body, called internal fertilization, or outside it, called external fertilization. The egg also has to stop more than one sperm getting in, which is called polyspermy. First comes a fast block: right after one sperm fertilizes the egg, the electrical charge across its membrane rapidly shifts and then returns to normal. A slow block begins within the first few seconds, as released calcium makes granules in the egg release enzymes that cause its outer membrane to swell and harden, keeping other sperm out.

paragraphs.heading: Cleavage
paragraphs.text: Next comes cleavage: the zygote divides again and again by mitosis without growing, so the cluster of cells stays the size of the original zygote. At least four divisions take place, giving a tightly packed ball of sixteen or more cells, called the morula. The cells made by cleavage, up to the blastula stage, are called blastomeres. Once the seventh division has produced 128 cells, the morula has become a blastula.

paragraphs.heading: Not every animal divides alike
paragraphs.text: Cleavage does not look the same in every animal. In holoblastic cleavage, all the cells divide, the division furrow runs across the whole cluster, and the whole cluster ends up as the embryo. In meroblastic cleavage only some cells divide, as the furrow does not reach into the yolky region, and some cells become the yolk sac. Animals also differ in the geometry of the furrow, which can be radial, spiral, bilateral or rotational.

paragraphs.heading: Blastula, gastrula and beyond
paragraphs.text: A blastula is usually a ball made of a single sheet of cells, the blastoderm, around a cavity filled with fluid or yolk called the blastocoel. Mammals at this point form a blastocyst, which has an inner cell mass set apart from the surrounding ball. In most animal groups the blastula then goes through gastrulation and becomes a gastrula, which has two cell layers in some species and three in most. The gastrula develops further, including organogenesis, the forming of organs. The embryo then moves on to its next stage, which differs between species: a fetus or a larva, for example.
